title: Skills redistribution: Human capabilities rise beside AI
desc: Reports employer expectations for automation, training, hiring and redeployment rather than realized profession-wide contraction.

kps.k: The cluster frames AI as a driver of job redistribution and changing skills, not uniform employment contraction.
kps.d: The Future of Jobs Report 2025 projects that AI and information-processing technologies will create 11 million jobs and displace 9 million during 2025–2030. It separately forecasts 19 million jobs created and 9 million displaced through broader digital access, and a net loss of approximately 5 million from robotics and autonomous systems. These distinct categories should not become a single AI displacement estimate. The report also attributes workforce change to economic uncertainty, geopolitical fragmentation, demographics and the green transition.

kps.k: The evidence captures employer expectations, not realised displacement or established AI causation.
kps.d: The report draws on more than 1,000 employers representing over 14 million workers across 22 industry clusters and 55 economies. Its 2025–2030 projections describe anticipated outcomes and workforce plans. Occupational growth percentages use current employment in each role as their denominator, and net growth subtracts displacement from creation. This evidence informs workforce scenarios but does not establish that AI has already caused the forecast changes.

kps.k: Contrasting lawyer forecasts qualify claims of universal legal-sector decline.
kps.d: One regional profile projects a 10% net decline in lawyers, while an economy profile projects 11% net growth; both show a global comparison of 2% net growth. The supplied excerpts do not identify those locations or isolate AI's contribution. The tension here concerns variation within one report, not disagreement between independent sources. Broad professional-services forecasts likewise cannot establish law-firm-specific staffing outcomes.

kps.k: Employers expect technical capability and human-centred skills to gain importance together.
kps.d: AI and big data, cybersecurity and technological literacy lead the report's global skill ranking, alongside creativity, adaptability and lifelong learning. These rankings measure the balance of employers expecting increasing versus decreasing skill use, not growth in employment or proficiency. In professional services, 98% expect AI and big data skills to become more important, while the profile forecasts technical-role growth and administrative-role decline. The implication is a changing mix of roles and capabilities rather than a simple substitution of technology for all professional work.

kps.k: Workforce plans combine automation with training, hiring, augmentation and redeployment.
kps.d: The report's global benchmarks show 85% of employers planning upskilling, 73% automation, 70% hiring for new skills, 63% technological augmentation and 51% transitions from declining to growing roles. Professional-services employers report 88% for upskilling, 75% for hiring and 70% for augmentation. These plans suggest that workforce preparation extends beyond headcount reduction, but skills gaps and organisational resistance may constrain execution. They remain employer intentions, not evidence that these strategies succeed.

vlens.an: The supplied market-analysis/consultancy evidence supports the proposition that AI is expected to redistribute work and skills rather than cause uniform employment contraction. The Future of Jobs Report 2025 forecasts job creation alongside displacement and anticipates rising demand for technical capabilities together with creativity, adaptability and other human-centred skills. It also reports employer plans that combine automation with upskilling, hiring, augmentation and redeployment. Material internal variation reinforces the proposition’s qualifications: lawyer projections differ substantially by geography, and broad professional-services forecasts cannot establish law-firm-specific outcomes. Moreover, the evidence consists of surveyed employer expectations and intended strategies for 2025–2030, not observed displacement, proven AI causation or demonstrated success of workforce interventions. Because the curated evidence here contains one report, this position should not be treated as representative of all market analysts, consultancies or press sources.

elens.an: The 2025 source supports the proposition that AI is expected to redistribute work and alter skill requirements rather than produce uniform employment contraction. Its employer forecasts combine job creation with displacement, rising demand for technical capabilities alongside creativity, adaptability and other human-centred skills, and workforce plans spanning automation, upskilling, hiring, augmentation and redeployment. Material internal variation reinforces rather than undermines this position: lawyer projections range from net decline in one unidentified regional profile to net growth in another economy profile, while broad professional-services data indicate technical-role growth and administrative-role decline but cannot establish law-firm-specific outcomes. The evidence is prospective and survey-based—employer expectations and plans for 2025–2030—not observed displacement, proof of successful workforce adaptation or established AI causation. Because the curated evidence here comprises one report, it should not be treated as representative of all employers or professions.
